items.title: The History and Labor of Web Scraping
items.abstract: Abstract Both the free labor of generating data online and the importance of data work which cleans, labels, and verifies these data are required for producing artificial intelligence (AI) systems. Between these two essential moments in AI production, we identify web scraping as the intercalary process of extracting data from the internet at scale. In this chapter, we highlight the essential contributions of web scraping to the production of machine learning training datasets and show that scraping is a distinct category of software labor whose understanding is important for the political economy of AI. The chapter characterizes the labor involved in both the production of scraping software and the labor required to conduct scraping operations. We provide a critical historical assessment of scraping dating back to the 1990s, tracing the development of scraping from a technical requirement for indexing the web in early communication software, to its commercialization and contemporary use in the development and production of large language models. We further describe the conditions of the labor of scraping through the analysis of contemporary documentation: industry-specific blogs, discussion boards, market reports, and conferences. We argue that the economic utility of data is dependent on its transformation from web data into datasets, and that this transformation is achieved through the labor of scraping. We suggest that the increased legal and technical barriers to the practice frame the current web scraping labor ecosystem, continuously demanding new kinds of human expertise.

items.title: The Impact of AI on Game Development: A Scoping Review of Transformations, Career Implications, and Emerging Challenges
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly transforming the game industry by reshaping development processes, production workflows, and career structures. In this study, we present a scoping literature review examining the impact of AI on game development and employment within the industry, with particular attention to the perspectives of displacement, task transformation, and productivity effects. Drawing on academic research and industry reports published between 2020 and 2026, while retaining earlier foundational literature where relevant, this study analyzes how AI technologies such as generative AI, machine learning, procedural content generation, and large language models are integrated across major stages of game production, including game art, production management, programming, and live operations. Our findings indicate that AI can support efficiency, accelerate development cycles, and enable new forms of personalization and creative experimentation. At the same time, AI adoption may alter workforce dynamics by increasing the automation potential of routine and entry-level tasks, especially in areas such as asset creation and quality assurance. Rather than fully replacing workers, however, AI more commonly reconfigures job roles and increases demand for hybrid skill sets that combine technical knowledge, creativity, and AI literacy. Our study also identifies emerging opportunities in AI-assisted design, data analytics, and machine learning integration. Despite these benefits, AI adoption introduces important challenges related to employment polarization, intellectual property, workforce adaptation, ethical governance, and market concentration. We conclude that AI is fundamentally reshaping the game industry and highlight the need for balanced strategies that support innovation while preserving creative diversity, sustainable career pathways, and equitable access to technological opportunities. Overall, the strongest evidence concerns AI capabilities, workflow changes, and task-level transformation, whereas direct evidence of actual employment outcomes and long-term occupational change remains limited and uneven.

items.title: The impact of human-AI co-creation on perceived creativity in generative AI art: a serial mediation mechanism of psychological ownership, perceived agency, and creative flow
items.abstract: Introduction Generative AI is shifting digital art from one-step generation toward interactive human-AI co-creation. Across two between-subject experiments ( N = 600), we examined how creation mode and prespecified AI-involvement workflows related to perceived creativity. Methods In Study 1, participants completed digital art tasks under human-only creation, AI-only generation, or human-AI co-creation conditions. In Study 2, three workflows differing in AI involvement (low, moderate, high) were evaluated. Psychological ownership, perceived agency, creative flow, and perceived creativity were measured. Results In Study 1, human-AI co-creation produced higher perceived-creativity ratings than AI-only generation, with indirect effects consistent with a serial pathway through psychological ownership, perceived agency, and creative flow. In Study 2, the moderate-involvement workflow yielded higher perceived-creativity ratings and psychological states than the low- and high-involvement workflows. Discussion Perceived creativity in generative-AI art depends on how users experience contribution, control, and engagement during creation. Within the workflows tested, balancing generative assistance with consequential user choice fosters the most favorable subjective creativity evaluations.

items.title: THE LITERARY REPRESENTATION OF HUMANITY’S DECLINING SIGNIFICANCE IN CLIFFORD D. SIMAK’S NOVEL CITY
items.abstract: The article examines the representation of humanity’s declining relevance in Clifford D. Simak’s science fiction novel City, focusing on the philosophical implications of the gradual disappearance of humankind from the central position in Earth’s evolutionary and cultural development. Drawing upon posthumanist theory, ecocriticism, and literary analysis, the study explores the symbolic transformation of humans from dominant agents of civilization into mythical figures whose legacy is preserved and reinterpreted by intelligent dogs and robots. Special attention is paid to the narrative structure of the novel, in which the framing legends and episodic stories gradually undermine the reliability of human-centered historical narratives. Simak depicts technological progress not as the culmination of human achievement but as a process that ultimately renders humanity unnecessary within its own evolutionary trajectory. The emergence of autonomous robots, genetically enhanced animals, and alternative forms of intelligence illustrates the decentralization of the human subject and challenges traditional definitions of civilization, intelligence, and social organization. The article argues that City anticipates many key ideas of contemporary posthumanist thought by presenting humanity as only one temporary stage in the broader continuum of life rather than the ultimate goal of evolution. Furthermore, the novel’s ecological perspective emphasizes cooperation instead of domination, suggesting that sustainable existence depends upon mutual adaptation rather than human control over nature. Simak’s vision remains particularly relevant in the context of current discussions concerning artificial intelligence, environmental crises, and the ethical implications of technological development. The study concludes that City represents not simply the decline of humanity but the emergence of a more inclusive understanding of life, intelligence, and civilization that transcends anthropocentric limitations.

items.title: The Managerial Blind Spot Effect Explainable Machine Learning for Strategic Decision-Making
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is used in strategic decision-making; however, it is not clear whether the use of explainable machine learning leads to more managerial judgment when prediction accuracy is high. This study analyzes the proposed ‘Managerial Blind Spot Effect’ by combining predictive modelling with behavioural analysis applied to the IBM Telco Customer Churn dataset and the AI Decision Dependence and Cognitive Caution dataset. Several models, including Explanatory Boosting Machine (EBM), XGBoost, Random Forest and Neural Network, were tested, and the explanation produced by the native model EBM was enhanced by SHAP-based explanation. The behavioural results revealed that both Trust in AI and Cognitive Caution significantly contributed to an increase in AI Dependence. EBM delivered the best predictive performance with intrinsic transparency. The results highlight the importance of using explainable AI prediction models in conjunction with managerial judgment in dashboards.

items.title: The Mediating role of attitudes towards artificial intelligence in the effect of healthcare workers’ levels of cognitive flexibility on innovative work behaviour
items.abstract: BackgroundDigital transformation in healthcare requires healthcare professionals to adapt to emerging technologies and exhibit innovative work behaviors. Cognitive flexibility is an important individual characteristic that facilitates adaptation to change and innovation. However, the role of attitudes toward artificial intelligence in this relationship remains unclear.ObjectiveThis study aimed to examine the effect of healthcare professionals' cognitive flexibility on innovative work behavior and to determine the mediating role of attitudes toward artificial intelligence in this relationship.MethodsThe study employed a quantitative, cross-sectional, and correlational design. Data were collected from 532 healthcare professionals working in Konya, Türkiye, using convenience sampling. The Cognitive Flexibility Scale, Innovative Work Behavior Scale, and Artificial Intelligence Attitude Scale were used. Descriptive statistics, reliability analyses, Pearson correlation analysis, and bootstrap-based mediation analysis were conducted.ResultsCorrelation analyses revealed significant positive relationships among cognitive flexibility, attitudes toward artificial intelligence, and innovative work behavior (p < 0.001). Regression analyses demonstrated that cognitive flexibility significantly predicted both attitudes toward artificial intelligence (β=0.436, p < 0.001) and innovative work behavior (β=0.472, p < 0.001). Furthermore, bootstrap mediation analysis confirmed a statistically significant indirect effect of cognitive flexibility on innovative work behavior through attitudes toward artificial intelligence (β=0.097, 95% CI [0.075, 0.168], p < 0.001), indicating partial mediation.ConclusionsAttitudes towards artificial intelligence partially mediate the relationship between cognitive flexibility and innovative work behavior among healthcare professionals. Enhancing cognitive flexibility and fostering positive AI attitudes may contribute to supporting innovative practices and facilitating digital transformation in healthcare organizations.

items.title: The Moderating Effect of Gender on the Relationship Between Artificial Intelligence Usage, Behavioral Intentions, and Academic Engagement in Mathematics Education
items.abstract: In the age of technology, where the educational sphere and strategic advancements drive development, it is essential to understand the complex nature of gender and implement innovative tools to foster an inclusive learning environment and empower every learner. This study examines the moderating effect of gender on the relationships among Artificial Intelligence (AI) use, behavioral intentions, and academic engagement in mathematics education. Using a cross-sectional design, the study sampled 328 mathematics undergraduates from public universities in southwestern Nigeria. A structured online questionnaire hosted on Google Forms was used to collect data. The data collected were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). The results indicated that AI actual usage has a significant positive impact on behavioral academic engagement (BAE), and AI behavioral intention positively influences AI actual usage. Additionally, AI behavioral intention does not significantly influence BAE. Furthermore, AI social norms exerted large positive effects on actual AI use and behavioral intentions. In addition, gender moderates the relationship between AI behavioral intention and BAE, AI behavioral intention and AI actual usage, and AI actual usage and BAE. Therefore, educators should create specialized interventions that are responsive to the motivational and demotivational factors affecting both male and female students.

items.title: The next frontier in healthcare simulation is human-AI teaming
items.abstract: Abstract Background Across health professions, AI agents are moving out of the background and into clinical teams as collaborative entities. Yet healthcare simulation continues to conceptualise AI as a tool that serves the scenario rather than one that inhabits it. This framing is no longer adequate. The clinical environments we are preparing practitioners for demand that professionals learn to team with AI and not merely use it. Main body We contend that human-AI teaming (HAIT) is the next frontier for healthcare simulation education and research. The addition of AI agents to human teams fundamentally alters how teams communicate, work together, and accomplish goals and therefore, by extension, how we must design simulation systems for education and research. We identify five dimensions of teamwork that AI is reshaping and discuss what each means for simulation practice: communication and information exchange, shared mental models, trust calibration, team reflexivity, and team performance. We then present five imperatives that healthcare simulation must address to meet the challenges and opportunities HAIT introduces: fidelity, assessment, ethics, governance, and medico-legal framing, curriculum and faculty development, and transfer of learning. Together, these ten domains constitute a research and education agenda for a field built on the science and art of preparation. Conclusion HAIT is an emerging clinical reality and the next frontier for healthcare simulation. We call on the simulation community to treat it as a first-order priority and to focus on developing fidelity standards for AI agents in simulation, validating human-AI teaming assessment tools, establishing ethical frameworks for AI-inclusive scenario design, investing in curriculum and faculty development, and committing to the research needed to establish whether HAIT-based simulation training translates into improved performance in AI-augmented clinical practice.

items.title: THE ROLE OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN DEVELOPING PROFESSIONAL COMMUNICATION COMPETENCE IN ESP
items.abstract: This thesis examines the role of artificial intelligence (AI) in developing professional communication competence among students studying English for Specific Purposes (ESP). It explores how AI-powered tools can support the development of speaking, writing, vocabulary, and interactional skills required in professional environments. Particular attention is paid to personalized learning, simulated professional communication, and immediate feedback. The thesis also considers the challenges associated with AI integration, including the reliability of generated information, overdependence on technology, and academic integrity. It argues that the effective use of AI, combined with teacher guidance and learner autonomy, can contribute to preparing students for professional communication in English.

items.title: THE ROLE OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN DOCUMENTING RELIGIOUS CULTURAL HERITAGE: A STUDY OF ITS POTENTIALS AND CHALLENGES
items.abstract: This study explores how artificial intelligence (AI) technologies can be employed to effectively enhance and document religious beliefs and practices. AI has the capability to process vast amounts of religious texts and sources, enabling the efficient extraction of significant information and patterns. Additionally, it facilitates the digitalization of religious heritage, ensuring its preservation for future generations. Smart applications also contribute to improving access to religious knowledge and fostering understanding between different cultures and religions. The use of AI in this field faces several challenges, including the need to consider the sensitivity of religious beliefs and rituals to avoid any negative reactions. Moreover, reliance on automated analysis may lead to the loss of cultural and spiritual context in traditional practices. Ensuring accuracy and avoiding bias is essential to preserving authentic values. Despite these challenges, AI offers promising opportunities for documenting religious heritage, provided that a balanced approach is adopted—one that acknowledges potential risks and respects the privacy and sanctity of religious beliefs.

items.title: The role of artificial intelligence in the modern Russian economy innovative development
items.abstract: Innovation is now not just one of the possible paths of development, but the main condition for the survival of any enterprise. The key factor that changes the paradigm of the innovation process is the ability to delegate routine operations. Previously, a significant portion of highly qualified employees’ time was spent on data collection and preliminary information processing, which considerably slowed down the research and development cycle. Modern technologies make it possible to completely delegate trivial tasks to intelligent systems, which are capable of processing such information much faster than a human. In today’s environment, the integration of autonomous intelligent systems is crucial for reducing operational costs. In 2026, artificial intelligence has transformed from an auxiliary technology into an indispensable tool for ensuring the competitiveness of knowledge intensive enterprises. The main areas of application of artificial intelligence have been analyzed, including the automation of business processes, generative design, and predictive analytics of production equipment. The main barriers that limit the implementation of automation systems based on artificial intelligence have been systematized and identified. It has been established that artificial intelligence has changed the methodology of research and development work, reducing the product development cycle from several months to several weeks. The conclusion is formulated that the integration of artificial intelligence tools into production processes reduces costs, the percentage of defective products, and requires staff to develop creative and strategic competencies. The role of artificial intelligence is defined not merely as an automation tool, but as an active participant in the innovation process, capable of creating innovative solutions. An author’s classification of barriers to the implementation of artificial intelligence in knowledge intensive industries has been developed.

items.title: The role of augmented reality in smart warehousing and supply chain optimisation
items.abstract: The rapid evolution of global supply chains (SC) under the Industry 4.0 (I4.0) paradigm has intensified the demand for efficiency, accuracy, and resilience in warehousing operations. Smart warehousing has emerged as a key driver of supply chain optimisation (SCO), integrating advanced digital tools to streamline inventory management, order fulfilment, and logistics coordination. Among these technologies, augmented reality (AR) has gained prominence due to its unique capability to enhance human performance by overlaying digital information onto the physical environment. Despite an increasing interest in related areas, there remains a lack of comprehensive understanding of how AR technologies are being integrated into SC initiatives under the I4.0 umbrella. To address this, the present study conducts a comprehensive bibliometric analysis of literature published between 2015 and 2025, using the “Web of Science” and “Scopus” databases as the primary sources. A total of 51 peer-reviewed articles were identified using a structured search query combining terms related to AR, I4.0, and SC optimisation. This work contributes by offering a comprehensive synthesis of the opportunities, challenges, and future directions of AR in smart warehousing. It provides actionable insights for researchers, practitioners, and policymakers seeking to leverage AR as a strategic tool for SC optimisation in the era of I4.0.

items.title: The Role of Digital Capabilities and Human Factors in Enhancing Port Service Performance: A Mediated Model for Eastern Indonesia
items.abstract: This research was conducted in response to the increasingly urgent need for digital transformation in port services in Eastern Indonesia to improve efficiency, transparency, and service quality amid the development of information technology. The research addresses a significant gap by integrating digital capabilities and human factors within the context of port digital transformation in Eastern Indonesia, an underexplored area in the existing literature. The research objective was to examine the influence of digital capabilities, human factors, and information system success on improvements in port service performance. The research method used a quantitative approach, with surveys of service users and system managers to measure technology acceptance and information system success. The number of respondents was 189. The use of a quantitative approach, including surveys and SEM-PLS analysis, is appropriate for testing complex relationships among variables. Based on the measurements, service performance (SP) obtained the highest score (R² = 0.732), supported by the organization's strong digital capabilities, effective human resources, and successful implementation of information systems. The anticipated outcomes include identifying critical factors that determine the success of digital transformation and developing an integrative model to guide the effective implementation of port services. The model linking digital capabilities, human factors, information system success, and port service performance provides a valuable framework for future empirical research.

items.title: The Role of Information Technology in Enhancing Customer Engagement in the Insurance Sector
items.abstract: The global insurance industry is undergoing a fundamental transformation, transitioning from rigid, product-centric operating models to agile, customer-centric ecosystems. Information Technology (IT) is the primary catalyst in this evolution, empowering insurers to connect with, understand, and serve their policyholders with unprecedented depth and precision. Traditional insurance models have long been characterized by impersonal interactions, fragmented data environments, slow response cycles, and a conspicuous absence of personalized service offerings—factors that collectively erode customer trust, engagement, and loyalty. This paper explores the multifaceted role of IT in enhancing customer engagement within the insurance sector, grounded in both academic literature and extensive practitioner experience across life, health, and annuity insurance domains. We propose a comprehensive conceptual framework that integrates diverse IT innovations—including Policy Administration Systems (PAS), unified customer data platforms, digital self-service portals, data analytics, artificial intelligence (AI), Application Programming Interfaces (APIs), cloud infrastructure, and omnichannel communication tools—to foster deeper, more meaningful, and enduring customer relationships. Our contribution is fourfold: first, we delineate a practitioner-informed conceptual framework for an IT-enabled customer engagement strategy in insurance, emphasizing omnichannel presence, data-driven personalization, and end-to-end policy lifecycle integration. Second, we examine the transformative potential of specific IT innovations, including AI-powered chatbots, predictive analytics engines, personalized digital portals, IoT-driven engagement, and cloud-hosted document management systems. Third, we contextualize these innovations through real-world implementation patterns observed across leading insurance carriers and reinsurers. Fourth, we discuss the strategic implications, implementation challenges, and actionable recommendations for insurers seeking to enhance customer loyalty, satisfaction, and long-term retention. By strategically leveraging IT and aligning technology investments with the customer journey, insurance companies can transcend transactional relationships and build enduring, value-driven connections with their policyholders—ultimately driving sustainable business growth and competitive advantage.

items.title: The Second Generation of AI / Второе поколение ИИ
items.abstract: An essay from The Bush Book. The smarter the model, the harder it is to spot an error in its text. A hybrid text is written by a human and a machine, creators of different natures who only seem to speak one language; it is fast, scalable, instrumental, and its errors may be contagious for people and for future models. The machine's answer is a "blank" that both work on, and both make mistakes; AI also carries people beyond their own competence, often under time pressure. The essay proposes a different basis for AI generations: not power or speed, but whether the human and the machine, working as one system, do no harm. The first generation extends a person; the second extends and protects, preventing errors before the signature reaches people. The image is the generations of fighter aircraft: the pilot must come home. Grows out of "The Snake's Tongue". A companion open specification sets out the idea in testable form. items.title: The Semiotics of AI-Generated Brand Narratives
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping the symbolic architecture of brand storytelling, introducing new dynamics in how meaning is constructed, circulated, and interpreted. As tools like large language models and text-to-image generators become embedded in branding practices, they influence not only the production of content but the semiotic processes that define brand identity and consumer engagement. This chapter presents a conceptual framework for understanding AI-generated brand narratives as co-authored expressions shaped by algorithmic grammar, cultural codes, and audience interpretation. The framework emphasises the shift from human-centric storytelling to hybrid narrative systems, where machine-mediated outputs carry embedded signs, stylistic cues, and symbolic intent. It also addresses tensions around authenticity, emotional resonance, and brand coherence.The framework offers a theoretical lens for analysing how generative AI transforms brand meaning, positioning it as both a technological and cultural force in contemporary marketing communication.

items.title: The Speaker Under Surveillance
items.abstract: This chapter examines how language operates within the postdigital environment, where communication increasingly takes place through online platforms shaped by algorithms and data systems. It reconsiders language as a system of signs that is no longer stable, as the relationship between speaker and listener is constantly shifting under conditions of surveillance and digital mediation. The discussion introduces the idea of a “void in semiosis” to explain the growing gaps, ambiguities, and disruptions in meaning-making processes. It further argues that platforms collect behavioral data and reorganize communication into prestructured forms, influencing how individuals express thoughts and emotions. The chapter also reflects on how capitalist systems and artificial intelligence reshape linguistic practices by limiting spontaneity and embedding control within communication networks. In this changing environment, language becomes less personal and more regulated, raising concerns about the future of human expression, agency, and the diversity of linguistic experience.

items.title: The System Hallucination Scale (SHS): A Human-Centered Instrument for Assessing Perceived Reliability of Large Language Models
items.abstract: Large language models routinely produce factually incorrect or misleading outputs, yet conventional automated benchmarks overlook how users perceive reliability during interaction. We introduce the System Hallucination Scale (SHS), a lightweight instrument modeling the famous System Usability Scale (SUS) and System Causability Scales (SCS). SHS measures perceived reliability across five dimensions: factual accuracy, source reliability, logical coherence, deceptiveness of presentation, and responsiveness to user guidance, using ten balanced Likert-scale items that provide a directional score and consistency diagnostic. In a supervised validation study with 193 participants (386 evaluations across 47 trained experimenters), SHS demonstrated strong internal consistency and high clarity, completing in an average of 4.2 minutes. Participants rated source verifiability and presentation deceptiveness worse than factual accuracy, indicating perceived vulnerabilities lie primarily in traceability and framing. As a proof of concept, SHS assesses human-perceived reliability rather than ground-truth correctness, providing open-source multilingual implementations and an interactive calculator.

items.title: Through the looking glass: an empirical study of users’ experiences of the regulatory framework governing text and data mining and some practical ways forward
items.abstract: Text and data mining (TDM) refers to the process of uncovering knowledge from datasets using computational analysis. Applications of TDM have grown rapidly in recent years, especially with the ever-growing popularisation of Artificial Intelligence. TDM sheds light on knowledge hidden in the shadows, unlocking insights that drive discovery and innovation. TDM practices are governed by a complex patchwork of regulatory frameworks that encompasses several areas of law, not always specifically attuned towards regulating TDM, such as contract law, copyright and data protection and privacy regulatory frameworks. Doctrinal research in this context has been increasing in popularity in recent years, examining the legal frameworks, which collectively regulate TDM practices. However, socio-legal research in this regard is still emerging. This study, through 11 semi-structured interviews with users who have experience with conducting TDM, provides novel insights into users’ experiences with the regulatory frameworks that govern their practices. It offers valuable insights into the dynamics of TDM, including the strategies and motivations driving regulatory compliance. It also highlights how the current regulatory structure could be refined to create a more balanced approach; one that effectively regulates TDM while safeguarding the interests of all stakeholders. Drawing on the study's findings, a set of recommendations are proposed, which aim to enable compliance with the existing regulatory framework for users, while still fostering both innovation and protection of stakeholder interests.

items.title: To airt – Proposal for an English Verb for Interacting with Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: “To airt” is proposed as an English verb for asking, prompting, consulting, or guiding an artificial intelligence in order to obtain information, ideas, advice, explanations, or other results. Example uses include: “Just airt it.”, “I already airted it.” and “Try airting it differently.” The proposal addresses an emerging lexical gap in everyday language. While “to google” provides a concise verb for searching the web, interaction with systems such as ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, and other AI systems is commonly described using longer or provider-specific expressions. The proposed AI-related meaning of “to airt” has an additional semantic connection to the historical Scots verb “airt”, which is attested with meanings related to directing, guiding, or pointing the way. In prompting an AI, a user likewise gives direction to an artificial intelligence. The spelling also visibly begins with “AI”. This publication does not claim the word “airt” itself as a new coinage. It proposes and documents a new AI-related meaning and usage of the existing verb. The proposal was developed as an English counterpart to the German neologism “kinstlern”, proposed by the same author in August 2026 to mean “to ask or consult an AI”. The proposed usage is intended for general and unrestricted use.

items.title: Towards a Next Generation of Accounting Information Systems: A Systematic Literature Review Approach
items.abstract: Accounting Information Systems (AISs) are central to organisational decision-making, financial reporting, and regulatory compliance. Yet, the rapid digitalisation of financial operations has exposed these systems to cyber vulnerabilities, human errors, and inefficiencies in data management. To systematically examine these weaknesses, this paper employs a Systematic Literature Review guided by the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) framework, analysing peer-reviewed journals, conference proceedings, and industry reports published between 2015 and 2025. The review identifies critical AIS vulnerabilities, including inadequate cyber controls, low human awareness of security risks, weak protection of digital assets, limited integration of risk management, absence of quantitative performance metrics, and restricted accessibility for Small and Medium-sized Enterprises (SMEs). Based on these findings, a structured framework for next-generation AIS solutions is proposed, comprising real-time dashboards, cloud-based zero-trust architectures, hyper-automation, artificial intelligence-driven insights, blockchain, Internet of Things integration, self-healing systems, and adaptive risk engines. These interventions aim to strengthen data integrity, system resilience, regulatory compliance, and organisational agility, offering practical benefits to SMEs and large organisations operating in increasingly complex financial environments. Overall, the paper provides a comprehensive, evidence-based roadmap that bridges gaps in cybersecurity, operational efficiency, and decision-making within AIS, contributing valuable insights for practitioners, researchers, and policymakers seeking to modernise AISs while mitigating cyber, operational, and compliance risks.

items.title: Training on the Standard, Judged by the Standard: The Benchmarking Paradox and Validation’s Impossibility in Human-LLM Co-Production
items.abstract: I built validation frameworks for Large Language Model (LLM) use in qualitative research and discovered that the more rigorously I validated, the more impossible validation became. This article theorises structural impossibility as the benchmarking paradox : LLMs train on human-generated text, then researchers validate outputs against human interpretation, which was the training source. Human interpretation functions simultaneously as training data, evaluation standard and outcome judged. Through diffractive reading of an empirical encounter where ChatGPT analysed policy texts, including vernacular translations it generated, I develop three theoretical coordinates: mimetic recursion (exposing circular validation), function/meaning incommensurability (revealing interpretation’s always-already hybrid nature) and epistemic authority redistribution (showing how computational infrastructure stratifies whose knowledge production counts). Empirically, GPT-5’s sophisticated meta-analysis of its own vernacular renderings exposes alignment priors determining computational legibility: whose voices register as analysable, which linguistic forms count as legitimate and what inquiries remain thinkable. The article argues that co-production through LLMs does not democratise qualitative research – it risks amplifying existing hierarchies while obscuring their operation through technical discourse. Rather than pursuing impossible validation, qualitative research should ask whose interpretive labour trained the pattern, contest whose interests human-LLM assemblages serve and demand that computational mediation generates epistemic and linguistic justice rather than reproducing the hierarchies it obscures.

items.title: Transforming Engineering Education Through Artificial Intelligence: Enhancing Learning, Innovation, and Student Engagement
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as an important component of contemporary engineering education, offering opportunities to improve learning outcomes through data-driven instructional approaches.Technologies such as machine learning, intelligent tutoring systems, natural language processing, learning analytics, and generative AI facilitate personalised learning, automated evaluation, continuous progress tracking, and practical simulation-based experiences.This study presents the Artificial Intelligence-Driven Engineering Education Framework (AIEEF), developed to examine the impact of AI-enabled educational practices on student learning, engagement, and innovation.The framework was evaluated through a systematic review of existing research and empirical analysis of educational performance indicators.The results indicate notable improvements in student achievement, engagement, and participation in creative activities following the implementation of the proposed framework.Among the predictive models examined, Gradient Boosting achieved an accuracy of 94.2%, while overall student engagement increased from 68.7% to 89.8%.The study also considers challenges associated with AI adoption, including data privacy, algorithmic fairness, and academic integrity.The findings suggest that carefully designed AIsupported learning environments can enhance engineering education and assist institutions in preparing graduates for emerging technological and industrial requirements.

items.abstract: Purpose: This study aims to develop a data-driven predictive framework to assess and forecast respiratory morbidity risks associated with air pollution and climate variability across the UAE, addressing the gap in region-specific health-environment models. Design/Methodology/Approach: Using environmental data from the National Centre of Meteorology (NCM) and health data from the Ministry of Health and Prevention (MOHAP), machine learning models, namely Random Forest (RF), Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), will be applied to analyse time-series data integrating air pollutants, namely Particulate Matter ≤ 2.5 μm (PM₂.₅), Particulate Matter ≤ 10 μm (PM₁₀), Nitrogen Dioxide (NO₂), Sulphur Dioxide (SO₂), Ozone (O₃), Carbon Monoxide (CO), together with meteorological factors (temperature, humidity, wind speed). Findings: The expected outcome is an explainable AI system capable of issuing early warnings for high-risk respiratory health days, improving predictive accuracy through multi-factor integration. items.title: Turkish yoga consumers’ motivation: A scale development study
items.abstract: In the growing yoga market, the purchasing behavior of yoga consumers constitutes one of the important research areas. Turkey is a new market for yoga. Information on the reasons and motivations of consumers in this market for purchase of yoga-related services/products is quite limited. For this reason, this study aims to develop a valid and reliable scale to determine the motivations of yoga consumers in Turkey to participate in yoga. The study was structured based on the Scale Development Process. A three-stage process consisting of Item Development, Scale Development and Scale Evaluation was carried out. As a result of the study, a scale consisting of 5 dimensions and 24 items was obtained. The scale shows that yoga consumers in Turkey have intrinsic motivations related to escape and achievement and extrinsic motivations related to visibility, socialization and reference. We hope that the scale developed in this study will contribute to the field in terms of identifying and making sense of the motivations of yoga consumers in similar markets such as Turkey, where yoga is/will be newly developing.

items.title: Ubuntu, African Ethics, and Human-Centred Artificial Intelligence in Project Management: A Systematic Literature Review
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is progressively revolutionising project management by enhancing forecasting, planning, decision-making, risk evaluation, and organisational efficacy. Nevertheless, escalating apprehensions about trust, accountability, equity, transparency, and human supervision have underscored the necessity for governance strategies that transcend mere technical efficacy. This research performs a concept-focused systematic literature review to investigate the convergence of Ubuntu, African ethics, Human-Centred Artificial Intelligence (HCAI), and project governance. This research consolidates disparate knowledge domains related to responsible AI, HCAI, ethical leadership, stakeholder governance, organisational preparedness, and Ubuntu-informed leadership, stakeholder inclusivity, and a comprehensive Ubuntu-informed human-AI governance framework, utilising peer-reviewed literature from 2022 to 2026. This research posits that Ubuntu offers a unique governance viewpoint rooted in collective responsibility, relational leadership, and human dignity. The results indicate that Ubuntu-informed AI governance can assist African governments and policymakers in establishing ethical and responsible frameworks. This research establishes a basis for subsequent investigations on Ubuntu, artificial intelligence governance, and project management. The results underscore the significance of ethical leadership, stakeholder engagement, human supervision, and responsibility for project management professionals in responsible AI-driven project settings.

items.title: Understanding ChatGPT adoption among medical students: an integrated theoretical model of psychological barriers and individual factors
items.abstract: Background The growing adoption of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), particularly ChatGPT, has created new opportunities for medical education by supporting learning, problem-solving, and knowledge acquisition. However, evidence regarding the psychological and individual factors influencing ChatGPT adoption among medical students remains limited. This study develops and tests an integrated theoretical model that combines Privacy Theory, Technostress Theory, Affect Theory, Diffusion of Innovation Theory, and the Theory of Planned Behavior to explain ChatGPT adoption. Material and methods A quantitative cross-sectional study was conducted among undergraduate medical students at King Faisal University, Saudi Arabia using a structured, self-administered questionnaire. The proposed model examined the effects of privacy concern, technophobia, guilt feelings, and innovativeness on behavioral intention and ChatGPT usage behavior, with behavioral intention serving as the mediating variable. Data were analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM). Results The findings showed that innovativeness had a significant positive relationship with behavioral intention ( β = 0.579, p < 0.001), while behavioral intention had a strong positive relationship with ChatGPT usage behavior ( β = 0.777, p < 0.001). In addition, behavioral intention significantly mediated the relationship between innovativeness and ChatGPT usage behavior ( β = 0.450, p < 0.001). In contrast, privacy concern, technophobia, and guilt feelings were not significantly related to behavioral intention, and their indirect relationships with ChatGPT usage behavior were also not significant. Conclusion Within the proposed model, personal innovativeness was the only antecedent significantly associated with behavioral intention, whereas the psychological barriers were not statistically significant. By integrating five complementary theoretical perspectives into a single framework, this study extends current understanding of generative AI adoption in medical education and highlights behavioral intention as the key mechanism linking individual characteristics to actual use. The findings provide theoretical insights and practical guidance for promoting the responsible and effective integration of ChatGPT into medical education through initiatives that foster innovativeness and AI literacy.

items.title: Understanding Social Bias in Multimodal Learning Systems: A Taxonomy and Framework
items.abstract: The rapid adoption of multimodal learning systems across high-stakes applications has intensified concerns about fairness and social bias, yet existing research remains scattered across modalities, tasks, protected attributes, mitigation strategies, and evaluation methodologies. This survey provides an overview of fairness and social bias in multimodal artificial intelligence. By reviewing 44 papers and 16 datasets, we synthesize the current landscape of fairness research in multimodal systems and identify emerging challenges and research opportunities. Our primary contribution is twofold. First, we introduce a multi-dimensional taxonomy that organizes the literature across nine operational dimensions, providing a unified perspective on multimodal fairness research. Second, we propose an end-to-end operational lifecycle framework that illustrates how biases emerge within shared latent spaces and identifies targeted pre-processing, training-time, and post-training intervention strategies. Overall, this survey discusses key performance-fairness trade-offs and provides a structured roadmap for evaluating and mitigating bias, ultimately supporting the development of more equitable multimodal AI systems.

items.title: Unexpected Encounters and Methodological Turns: Navigating the Ethical Implications of Artificial Intelligence’s Unanticipated Presence in Qualitative Scholarship
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has been a silent presence in research for several years, and through various technologies, AI has become ever-present in qualitative studies. As AI continues to proliferate and its use expands both outside and within scholarship, the use of AI in research has evolved from a resource for qualitative scholars to a tool for study participants to use as they engage with our research studies. We had separate encounters with research participants using AI to author narratives in our dissertation studies. Through examples from our studies, this article explores the impact of AI use by study participants.

items.title: User Preferences for Enhanced Robot Adaptation in Assistive Tasks
items.abstract: The adaptation of robot behaviour to each user can be seen as an ergonomic feature. Adaptation plays a key role in increasing human–robot interaction efficiency and safety, and this is especially relevant in assistive scenarios, where users may be unable to adapt to the robot or help in task execution. Robot adaptation may happen at different levels of abstraction, from low-level trajectory parameters to higher-level task concepts. These higher-level abstractions relate to human factors such as personal preferences on how the robot should perform the task. This chapter introduces the concept of user preferences to adapt the robot’s behaviour and also help in the robot’s decision-making, with a special focus on assistive robotic tasks such as dressing or feeding a user with mobility impairments. It also presents the challenges associated with adaptation in this kind of scenario, as well as some existing methods that may be used to adapt robot behaviour to high-level abstract preferences. Such adaptation makes it easier for the user to interact with the robot in a more efficient and comfortable manner, thus improving its ergonomics.

items.title: User-Centred Ecological Interface Design (UCEID)
items.abstract: User-Centred Ecological Interface Design (UCEID) is a human factors framework designed to be used in the early stages of interface design. This suite of methods was used to determine what features Mobility as a Service (MaaS) required to not only be a genuinely useful and effective journey planning tool but also accessible to all ages and genders to ensure travel equity. Methods used included benchmarking MaaS apps, holding focus groups looking at in-app iconography, and Design with Intent workshops leading to design concepts and storyboards. As a result, design recommendations were provided to optimise the initial product design.

items.title: Validation of a computer-vision milking parlour monitoring system
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence can help identify suboptimal milking practices and provide reports without time-consuming visits. The objective of this study was to validate a computer-vision milking parlour monitoring system (CVS, Cattle Care Inc.) by comparing its reports against trained human observers (n = 2, comparison method). A camera was installed in the parlour of two dairy farms in Ontario, Canada, one operating a herringbone parlour and the other a parallel parlour. Four one-hour segments (2 per farm), selected by the CVS, were independently analysed by human observers and the CVS. Prep-lag time, average unit-on time, turn time, and milking protocol deviations were assessed in each shift and compared between methods. For continuous variables, Lin’s concordance correlation coefficients (CCC) were calculated to evaluate the agreement between CVS and human observers; Bland–Altman plots were used to assess systematic bias. For categorical variables, the F-score was calculated to assess event-detection performance. The CCC for unit-on time (n=44 milking turns) was 0.999 (95% CI: 0.999-0.999), for prep-lag time (n = 214 cows) was 0.995 (95% CI: 0.994–0.996) and for turn time (n = 25 turns) was 0.998 (95% CI: 0.997–0.999). All protocol deviations flagged by the human observers (n = 51 events) were detected by the CVS; six towel misuse events detected by the CVS were missed by the human observers. An F-score of 1 was obtained for the CVS method. Under the conditions tested, the CVS demonstrated high agreement with human observations for prep-lag time, unit-on time, turn time, and milking-protocol deviations, while also identifying some events not detected by human observers. The assessed technology may complement human expertise by enabling more efficient and streamlined assessment of milking parlour performance.
